reader.title: Lynching of John Ninna and Slume
bases: A party of 45-80 settlers seized two Kootenai men and hanged them for an alleged murder [A10, A15, A19].
Two men were hanged by a party of dozens of settlers who chose not to turn them over to the law [A10, A15], to punish an alleged killing of three prospectors [A6, A19].

A settler letter, the Missoulian account, an Idaho correspondent, a Minnesota correspondent and the Indian agent's report independently agree two Kootenais were hanged by settlers [A2, A10, A15, A6, A19].

summary.text: The lynching of John Ninna and Slume was the hanging of two Kootenai men by a party of white settlers north of Flathead Lake in Missoula county, Montana, in March 1888, at a place a settler's letter called Penny's mill.
The settlers accused them of joining in the killing of three white prospectors on Wolf Creek the previous summer; a third accused man escaped.
The hanging set off a brief settler alarm and a petition for troops, but no hostilities were reported and later accounts called the scare exaggerated.

In mid-March a Missoulian correspondent at Sheldon wrote that settlers were agitated over the discovery that six Kootenais had killed three men camped on Wolf prairie the previous June and burned the bodies, and that white men were arming to pursue them.
A Thompson Falls correspondent identified the missing men as Ben Thompkins, one Johnson and Daniel McDonald, who had left Libby to prospect on July 1, 1887.
Indian agent Ronan later reported that his inquiries led him to believe the settlers had identified the right men.

The fullest account, given to the Missoulian, said forty-five to fifty settlers gathered at Demersville early one morning and searched the Kootenai lodges below town until they found John Ninna and Slume asleep.
The two were rowed across the Flathead river and hanged from a tree limb on the east bank, and the bodies were later cut down and buried.
According to that account the settlers "resolved to hang the two Indians, instead of turning them over to the law and its uncertain results."
The third accused man, Antley, was warned by a rider from the camp and fled.
The Idaho Semi-Weekly World put the party at eighty men and wrote that a deputy sheriff briefly took the prisoners from it at "Demarville" before they were recaptured.
In that version Slume confessed in English, "the verdict was death," and the two were hanged one after the other with a single rope.
An Ashley dispatch dated the action March 19.
Afterward families gathered at G. M. Lakin's place, the Sheldon school house and Ashley, and armed men guarded the Point of Rocks, Lee's ferry and the Big Fork ford.
An armed company then met the Kootenai chief, Aeneas or Eneas, who according to several reports accepted the hanging and agreed to give up the third man if caught.
On April 11 a mass meeting at Ashley named a committee to petition the secretary of war for troops.
A Sheldon resident replied in the Helena Herald that there had never been any danger of an outbreak.

Ronan wrote that Eneas thought hanging the guilty was just but regretted that the settlers "took the law into their own hands," and he blamed a white traveler's false report of an armed band for the panic.
No report of an arrest, inquest or prosecution of the lynchers appears in the coverage.
The story first spread through the settler's letter, which ran in late March in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, the Helena Weekly Herald, the Butte Semi-Weekly Miner and the Livingston Enterprise.
These items framed it as an "Indian Scare" or "Indian Outbreak," and the Herald added that the Kootenais were "a revengeful tribe."

The Bozeman Weekly Chronicle headlined the Missoulian account "Two of the Three Kootenai Murderers Hanged to a Tree," and the Morris Sun in Minnesota ran "Lynching Bad Indians," saying the citizens had "made good Indians" of the prisoners.
Some papers voiced doubt. The New York Sun, writing of "Ponnls Mills," wondered whether innocent men had been lynched and said the settlers' alarm outweighed any satisfaction from their revenge.
The Philipsburg Mail judged the men probably guilty but said the affair should be investigated.
By May the Fort Benton River Press reported all quiet and called the request for troops unwise.

Accounts differ on custody: the Morris Sun said the men had been arrested on an Ashley warrant and that fifty or sixty citizens overpowered the deputy's guard, while the Missoulian account describes no arrest and Ronan said in September that the Ramsdale brothers caught the two and hanged them at once.
The place is given as Penny's mill in the settler's letter and as the east bank of the Flathead opposite Demersville in the Missoulian and Idaho accounts.

accounts.label: Settler's letter
accounts.gist: Two 'Indian murderers' lynched at Penny's mill; families gathered and crossings guarded for fear of a Kootenai outbreak.

accounts.label: Missoulian informant
accounts.gist: 45-50 settlers took Ninna and Slume from their lodges near Demersville and hanged them across the river; Antley escaped; the chief later accepted it.

accounts.label: Idaho correspondent
accounts.gist: Eighty men captured two; a deputy briefly took them; the party recaptured them, heard a confession and hanged them one at a time.

accounts.label: Morris Sun correspondent
accounts.gist: Two arrested on an Ashley warrant; 50-60 citizens overpowered the deputy's guard and took them across the river.

accounts.label: Indian agent Ronan
accounts.gist: Citizens executed two Kootenais whom he believed guilty; Eneas regretted the lynching; the alarm was false and exaggerated.

accounts.label: Sheldon resident
accounts.gist: No danger of outbreak ever existed; the chief was satisfied with the hanging.

framing.detail: Bozeman Weekly Chronicle: 'Two of the Three Kootenai Murderers Hanged to a Tree', 'bad Indians', little mourning.
Settler letter run as 'An Indian Scare' / 'On the War Path' / 'Indian Outbreak'.
Morris Sun 'Lynching Bad Indians': settlers 'made good Indians' of them.
New York Sun editorial asks whether innocent men were lynched and mocks the resulting panic.
Philipsburg Mail: probably guilty, but the affair should be investigated.
River Press: all quiet; alarm exaggerated; Indians 'had a lesson taught them'.
